You said:

in react there is no html file

ChatGPT said:

Yes, coco 💚 — React itself doesn't use an .html file for each page/component, but your React project still has one HTML entry file.

If you're using Vite + React, your project usually looks like:

Plain text
my-react-project/ ├── src/ │ ├── App.tsx │ ├── main.tsx │ └── ... ├── public/ ├── index.html ← this one ├── package.json └── ...

So you should have:

Plain text
index.html

in the project root, not inside src.

Why you might think there is no HTML

When you write React components:

TypeScript
const Home = () => {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Hello</h1>
    </div>
  )
}

you don't create:

Plain text
Home.html About.html Contact.html

Instead, React creates the UI from your components.

The basic flow is:

Plain text
index.html ↓ main.tsx ↓ App.tsx ↓ Components ↓ Browser UI

For Poppins

Open your index.html. You should see something similar to:

HTML
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />

    <title>My Portfolio</title>
  </head>

  <body>
    <div id="root"></div>
    <script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx"></script>
  </body>
</html>

You can put the Poppins <link> inside <head>:

HTML
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />

  <link
    href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Poppins:wght@400;500;600;700&display=swap"
    rel="stylesheet"
  />

  <title>My Portfolio</title>
</head>

Then in your CSS:

CSS
body {
  background: #344e41;
  font-family: "Poppins", sans-serif;
  padding: 12px 25px;
}

So React doesn't eliminate HTML. React mainly lets you build the HTML-like UI using JSX/TSX components instead of manually creating separate HTML pages.

You said:

border-radius: 50%; this in tailwind css

ChatGPT said:

Yes, coco 💚

In Tailwind CSS:

CSS
border-radius: 50%;

is:

TypeScript
rounded-full

Example

CSS:

CSS
img {
  border-radius: 50%;
}

Tailwind:

TypeScript
<img className="rounded-full" />

rounded-full gives you a fully rounded shape, which is commonly used to make a square image circular.

For example:

TypeScript
<img
  src={shwePhoto}
  className="w-40 h-40 rounded-full"
/>

Here:

  • w-40 → width
  • h-40 → height
  • rounded-full → border-radius: 50%

⚠️ For a perfect circle, make the width and height equal.

You said:

<img className=' w-112.5 h-112.5 rounded-full object-cover'src={shwePhoto}></img> It's doesn't show exact circle

ChatGPT said:

Yes, coco 💚. The issue is most likely w-112.5 and h-112.5.

In Tailwind, arbitrary/custom values need square brackets:

TypeScript
<img
  className="w-[450px] h-[450px] rounded-full object-cover"
  src={shwePhoto}
  alt="Shwe Htet Ei Win"
/>

Why?

You wrote:

TypeScript
w-112.5 h-112.5

Tailwind doesn't interpret 112.5 that way as a custom size.

If you want 450px × 450px, write:

TypeScript
w-[450px] h-[450px]

Then:

Plain text
450px width ↓ ┌─────────┐ │ │ │ IMAGE │ ← 450px │ │ └─────────┘ ↑ 450px height

And:

TypeScript
rounded-full

turns that square into a perfect circle.

One more important thing

If the outer shape is a circle but the person's face/photo looks stretched or oddly positioned, that's not rounded-full. That's controlled by:

TypeScript
object-cover

object-cover crops the image to fill the 450×450 circle while keeping the image's aspect ratio.

So I'd use:

TypeScript
<img
  className="w-[450px] h-[450px] rounded-full object-cover"
  src={shwePhoto}
  alt="Profile"
/>

If the circle itself is still not appearing perfectly round after this, show me the screenshot — then we can check the parent/container CSS too.

You said:

what is target_blank mean

ChatGPT said:

target="_blank" in HTML/React means open the link in a new browser tab.

For example:

TypeScript
<a href="https://github.com" target="_blank">
  GitHub
</a>

When the user clicks GitHub, the browser opens GitHub in a new tab instead of replacing your current portfolio page.

Common targets

HTML
target="_blank"

→ New tab

HTML
target="_self"

→ Same tab (default)

So for your portfolio's social icons, you might use:

TypeScript
<a href="https://github.com/yourusername" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" > GitHub </a>

The rel="noopener noreferrer" is recommended when using target="_blank" for security and privacy reasons.

In short:

Plain text
target="_blank" ↓ "Open this link in a new tab."
ChatGPT can make mistakes. Check important info.
